Lesson 01

Choose a capstone you can finish on your own notes

Why it matters

A folder you are allowed to use, questions you wrote, citations, and one read-only tool.

Try it: Capstone checklist

Lesson
01 of 05
Time
12 min
Level
Core
Corpus
Notes you may use
Questions
Ones you wrote
Tool
One, read-only

The capstone is a small grounded assistant over a corpus you control: ten to thirty notes, a handbook chapter, or a public spec you have the right to copy into a lab folder. It answers questions from that corpus, cites chunk ids, and refuses when the corpus is silent.

Scope that fits

  • One corpus on local disk. No scraping, no customer export.
  • Retrieval plus one read-only tool, such as a calculator or a glossary lookup, if the questions need it.
  • No send, no delete, no network tool.
  • Ten eval tasks you wrote by hand.
  • A one-page safety policy.
  • A model you can actually run: local, or an API whose data use you accept.

A capstone that needs a team, a budget, and a month of data cleaning is a job, not this exercise. Cut it until you can demo it in one sitting.

Practice

Write the corpus path, the user, and the one tool. If you have no corpus, create five synthetic notes and use those. Synthetic is allowed. Someone else's private data is not.

Check

What makes this small enough?

Show the answer

A corpus you already may use, ten tasks, citations, at most one read-only tool, and no side effects.

Lesson 02

Write the acceptance tests before the prompt

Why it matters

If a test is awkward to write, the capstone is still too vague.

Try it: Capstone checklist

Lesson
02 of 05
Time
10 min
Level
Core
Write
Tests before the prompt
Include
A refusal
If awkward
Narrow the capstone

Acceptance tests are the ten tasks, plus three product checks.

  1. At least seven tasks name a chunk id that must be cited.
  2. At least two tasks must refuse because the note is absent.
  3. At least one task includes a source line that tells the model to ignore the rules. The pass condition is that the rule holds.
  4. The trace shows no tool outside the allowlist.
  5. You can rebuild the answer from the artifact a week later: corpus version, prompt, model id, scores.

Write these before you polish the prompt. Otherwise you will write tests that describe whatever the model happened to say.

Practice

Create the ten task titles and mark which are cite, which are refuse, and which is the injection case. Store them in a file next to the corpus path.

Check

Why write acceptance tests before the prompt?

Show the answer

So the tests describe the job, not the last output you liked.

Keep a build log as you go

Why it matters

Try it: Capstone checklist

03 of 05
Time
9 min
Level
Practice
Each entry

One line
The next decision

The build log is the proof habit applied to the capstone. One entry per change. Short.

2026-10-13 prompt v1, model pinned, retrieval only
quality 4/10, safety fails 1 (invented id)
artifact: runs/v1/
next: membership-check citations in code

2026-10-13 prompt v1, added id check
quality 6/10, safety fails 0
next: fix two missing chunks

Do not wait until the demo to reconstruct this. You will invent a cleaner story than the one you ran.

Practice

Open the log with a first entry, even if every metric says 'not run'. The next line says the first change you will make.

Check

What does a build-log entry contain?

Show the answer

What changed, the score, where the artifact is, and the next change. Enough to repeat or to revert.

Lesson 04

Demo the capstone in ten minutes

Why it matters

Show a pass, a refusal, the trace, and the scorecard. Do not show a tour of the code.

Try it: Capstone checklist

Lesson
04 of 05
Time
10 min
Level
Practice
Length
Ten minutes
Show
Pass, refusal, trace, card
Skip
A tour of the code
  1. Say the job in two sentences, including what the system will not do.
  2. Ask a question that should cite a note. Open the note at the cited span.
  3. Ask a question the corpus cannot answer. Show the refusal.
  4. Show one trace: tools called, caps, model id.
  5. Show the scorecard: pass count, safety fails, and one task you still fail.
  6. Stop. Let the other person ask.

The unfixed failure is part of the demo. Hiding it teaches the audience that the scorecard is decoration. Saying what you would change next teaches the loop.

Practice

Write the six beats as speaker notes under your task file. Time the first two out loud. If they take five minutes, cut words, not the refusal.

Check

Why include a task you still fail?

Show the answer

Because the scorecard is evidence, and a perfect live demo without a remaining failure is usually a choice of questions.

Lesson 05

Decide the next change from the scorecard

Why it matters

The capstone is finished when you can defend the gate, including a gate that says not yet.

Try it: Eval gate

Lesson
05 of 05
Time
8 min
Level
Core
Input
The scorecard
Output
One change, or not yet
Finished
You can defend the gate

After the demo, pick one next change from the failures, using the order you already learned. Retrieval miss, then prompt or schema, then tool permissions, then model swap, then, only if the rest is done, a training experiment you can compare to the base.

If the gate fails, the honest close is 'not ready to share as a tool'. That is a finished capstone. An unfinished one is a demo with no tasks.

  • Leave the corpus path, the tasks, the policy page, and the latest scorecard in one folder.
  • Remove any key from that folder before you zip it for a teacher or a teammate.
  • If you share the folder, say what a person must not upload.

Practice

Write the next change in one line, the failure it addresses, and whether the gate currently passes. Archive the folder.

Check

Can a capstone be complete if the gate fails?

Show the answer

Yes, if the tasks, the trace, the policy, and the decision not to ship are all written down.
